name: James A. Garfield
role: U.S. Representative from Ohio (1863-1880) and 20th President of the United States (1881)
summary: Republican hard-money, Union-first politician who backed Black citizenship and suffrage, federal aid to universal education, a legally regulated civil service and a tariff for revenue with incidental protection. He was cautious about federal coercion in some Reconstruction measures and skeptical of unions and monopolies alike. Most modern-issue statements are anachronistic and left blank.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Described in the Wikipedia biography as generally a laissez-faire believer on the hard-money side of the Republican Party.

public-ownership.rationale: Inferred: described as a laissez-faire believer who wanted government kept to coinage, justice and modest aid.

unions-good.rationale: Wikipedia reports he opposed the power sought by labor unions.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Wikipedia says he opposed monopolistic corporate practices; no broader regulatory program found.

empower-police-military.rationale: No recorded position found: the evidence found addresses a nearby question, not this statement.

decide-locally.rationale: Rejected the doctrine of State supremacy and stressed national authority and enforcement of federal law, while affirming states keep local self-government.

traditional-family.rationale: No recorded position found: the evidence found addresses a nearby question, not this statement.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Inaugural pledges full and equal protection for freedpeople and universal education to lift the freed race; as president he appointed Black officials and proposed federal education aid.

free-trade.rationale: Retained protective customs duties for American producers rather than unrestricted trade.

central-planning.rationale: Inferred: laissez-faire outlook and hard-money views; he spoke of no state direction of the economy.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Inaugural address says the healthy growth of manufacturers should still be matured; the 1880 letter wants a tariff that raises revenue while letting American labor and capital compete fairly. Earlier he leaned toward freer trade, so support is moderate.

state-directs-investment.rationale: No recorded position found: the evidence found addresses a nearby question, not this statement.

one-party-rule.rationale: Demanded freedom for voters to support any party and effective minority-party checks.

democracy-best.rationale: Future of Republic, II:50–55: defended democratic principle.

right-to-secede.rationale: Inaugural: the war settled that the Constitution and laws are supreme and bind states; letter condemns the doctrine of State supremacy.

separate-church-state.rationale: Inaugural: no ecclesiastical organization may usurp any function of the national government; letter calls for absolute separation of church and state in taxation.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Negotiated the 1871 removal of the Bitterroot Salish to a reservation; contested treaty.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: College Education, I:269–271: industry advances civilization.

conscription.rationale: In Congress during the Civil War he pushed a conscription bill (without a commutation buy-out) with Lincoln support.

hereditarian-race.rationale: No recorded position found: the evidence found addresses a nearby question, not this statement.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Hawaiian Islands, II:320–321: rejected tropical annexation, excepted northern expansion.

school-vouchers.rationale: His letter opposes public funds for sectarian schools while backing federal aid to common schools.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Inferred: his letter backs paying down the debt and the inaugural address demands rigid economy in government spending.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Inaugural: freedpeople were entitled to equal citizenship and equal protection of the law, with no middle ground.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: No recorded position found: the evidence found addresses a nearby question, not this statement.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Inaugural: both races made equal before the law; no middle ground between slavery and equal citizenship.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: Denied ecclesiastical organizations any governmental authority; demanded enforcement of civil law despite religious scruples.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Inferred: he opposed public funds for sectarian schools and wanted church and state separate in taxation.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Inaugural says the Union is founded directly on the will of the people and calls government one of the people.

separated-powers.rationale: Pledged constitutional limits on his executive actions and cooperation with Congress.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: No recorded position found: the evidence found addresses a nearby question, not this statement.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Opposed the 1871 Ku Klux Klan Act partly over the president power to suspend habeas corpus, though he condemned the Klan.

party-controls-media.rationale: Press, II:579: condemned governmental press censorship.

head-commands-forces.rationale: No recorded position found: the evidence found addresses a nearby question, not this statement.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: No recorded position found: the evidence found addresses a nearby question, not this statement.

death-penalty.rationale: Inferred: in 1864 he advocated executing or banishing the leaders of the rebellion; wartime treason is not terrorism or the gravest crimes generally.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Inaugural: Congress should respect conscientious scruples but prohibit criminal practices such as polygamy; religion gives no exemption from general law.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Inaugural condemned the Mormon Church for usurping legal functions and wanted its practices prohibited; limited to that case.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Treated the Union victory in the Civil War as the settled answer to disunion, and backed the war effort and conscription.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Explicitly promised obedience to constitutional restrictions and laws.

ban-cartels.rationale: Opposed monopolistic corporate practices per Wikipedia; no specific cartel measure found.

history-own-civilization.rationale: College Education, I:272: prioritize American history.

patriotic-education.rationale: College Education, I:271–272: teach patriotic civic history.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Future of Republic, II:68: reform can avert collapse.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Inferred: from his view that press freedom lies beyond legislative interference (Press, vol. II); he did not address an entrenched bill of rights as such.

office-by-exam.rationale: Argued the civil service must be regulated by law and supported a federal civil service and an end to spoils pressure; no explicit mention of examinations in sources read.

corporate-influence.rationale: Future of Republic, II:61–62: condemned corporate capture; Crédit Mobilier involvement complicates his record.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Condemned intimidation and suppression of lawful political opposition in the South.

property-franchise.rationale: He treated ignorance among voters as a danger to be met by universal education, not by restricting the vote; he called violating the suffrage a crime.

racial-franchise.rationale: Inaugural: there can be no permanent disfranchised peasantry; denying the ballot is a crime; he praised the 15th Amendment.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Future of Republic, II:62–66: wealth subjugates government.

national-church-status.rationale: Revolution in Congress, II:661–662: no state-established religion.

no-business-privileges.rationale: Called federal land grants to railroads unjust and as president pursued the Star Route postal fraud involving well-connected contractors.

notes:
Born 1831, assassinated 1881. Tariff views shifted from freer trade after the Civil War toward revenue tariffs with protective effect. Bland-Allison and currency positions were read but no statement in the test addresses gold or silver directly. The Morey letter on Chinese labor is disputed and not used as evidence.

Merged with an independent gpt-6.1-sol audit: 27 answers taken from it, 10 agreed, 0 conflicts settled by the integrator.

gpt-6.1-sol notes: Independent pass; old answers not read. Both complete 1882 collected-speech volumes were downloaded as original OCR and searched by theme. Editorial introductions, quoted opponents and quoted Fourier or Macaulay are distinguished from Garfield’s own words. Chapter and printed page references accompany book-based rationales. The 1864 rebel-estate proposal does not establish general confiscation of landed estates; his 1876 discussion praises reconstruction without postwar confiscation. General land redistribution remains null. The alliance statement rests on his explicit 1870 endorsement, not merely an inferred preference from geography. Most other priority statements lack matching evidence; industrial independence is not proof that anticolonial independence requires economic revolution. Allegations of financial misconduct are not treated as established policy endorsements. Broad property, welfare-dependency, price-control and ownership theories remain unknown. Ecological searches found no matching conservation position; industrial optimism is not a blanket technology-solves-most-problems claim. Public support for education does not itself settle sex education or religious instruction. The forged Morey letter was not used. All remaining nulls reviewed against the complete statement list. Racial-mixture claims do not cancel his express support for equal Black citizenship; they do qualify any characterization of him as holding modern racial egalitarian views. The 1876 praise for leniency does not explicitly renounce the legal availability of capital punishment.
